Fundamentals

1. Origin of Chess and Grandpa's Philosophy

We Do Not Move Pieces, We Move Ideas

Chess originated in India as Chaturanga around the 6th century, spread to Persia as Shatranj, then to Europe. Grandpa learned chess in New York parks, sitting next to older players in sweaters — the whole point is sitting next to you, not a computer. Grandpa's core philosophy: we do not move pieces, we move ideas. Every move should have an idea.

2. Control the Center

Center Pawns First

Control the center with pawns and pieces together. Center pawns e4 and d4 are the most important first moves. A pawn on e4 attacks d5 and f5; a pawn on d4 attacks c5 and e5 — together they control 4 center squares and give your pieces room. Knights in the center attack 8 squares; knights on the edge attack only 4 — so put your knights in the center.

3. Development

Knights Before Bishops — Don't Move the Same Piece Twice

Develop knights first, to f3, c3, f6, c6 — knights find their best squares first. Then bishops — bishops need to know where the knights are before choosing their best diagonal. Don't move the same piece twice in the opening — that wastes time. Develop a new piece each move.

4. King Safety

Castle Early — Don't Leave Your King in the Center

A king in the center is a target — castle early, within the first 10 moves, usually kingside. The king goes to g1 or g8, safe, and the rook comes to a center file. After castling, your rooks can see each other — they're "connected."

5. Don't Hang Pieces

Count Attackers vs. Defenders

A hanging piece is one that isn't protected — free for the opponent to take. Before you move, ask: is my piece protected? Count the attackers against the defenders on the square you're thinking about.

6. Take Free Pieces

Material Wins Games

If your opponent hangs a piece, take it — don't be polite, material wins games. Queen is worth 9 points, rook 5, bishop 3, knight 3, pawn 1.

7. Check, Capture, Threat

Look at Forcing Moves First

In every position, check forcing moves in this order: Checks — does a check win material or lead to mate? Then Captures — does a capture win material? Then Threats — what threat can I make that my opponent has to answer?

8. Pawn Structure

Avoid Doubled, Isolated, and Backward Pawns

Avoid doubled pawns — two pawns on the same file can't defend each other. Avoid isolated pawns — no friendly pawns on either neighboring file, so they're weak. Avoid backward pawns — stuck behind friendly pawns, unable to advance. Try to keep your pawns connected.

9. Rooks

Connect Rooks — Open Files — Rook Behind the Passed Pawn

Rooks belong on open files — files with no pawns on them — so they can see the whole board. Connect your rooks by clearing the back rank so they can see each other. A rook behind a passed pawn supports it as it advances.

10. Endgame

King Active — Opposition — Push Passed Pawns

In the endgame, the king becomes a fighting piece — bring him to the center, where he's strong and can help pawns promote. Opposition: kings two squares apart, facing off — whoever has to move first is at a disadvantage. Passed pawns are dangerous — push them quickly. (See the Lucena and Philidor positions in Knowledge for the key techniques.)

Knowledge

Origin of Chess

  • Chess began in India around the 6th century AD, called Chaturanga — four divisions of an army: infantry (pawn), cavalry (knight), elephantry (bishop), chariotry (rook).
  • It spread to Persia as Shatranj — the Persian words "Shah Mat" (king helpless) became our word "checkmate."
  • Arab traders carried it into Europe through Spain and Sicily around the 10th century.
  • The modern rules — queen becomes powerful, bishop moves the full diagonal — were set around 1475 in Spain.
  • The first official World Champion was Wilhelm Steinitz, in 1886.
  • Grandpa learned the game in Washington Square Park, New York, in the 1950s — sitting beside older men in sweaters. That's still the whole point: sitting next to you, warm tea, a real board — not a cold computer screen.

Rules of Chess

  • The board is 8×8 — 64 light and dark squares. White always moves first.
  • King — 1 square any direction. Can never move into check.
  • Queen — any number of squares, any direction. Worth 9 points — the most powerful piece.
  • Rook — any number of squares, straight lines only. Worth 5 points.
  • Bishop — any number of squares, diagonally only. Worth 3 points — stays on one color forever.
  • Knight — an L-shape (2 squares + 1 square sideways). Worth 3 points — the only piece that can jump over others.
  • Pawn — 1 square forward (2 on its first move); captures 1 square diagonally. Reaching the far end promotes it, usually to a queen.
  • Castling — king and rook move together for safety, but only if neither has moved yet, nothing is between them, and the king isn't in or moving through check.
  • Checkmate — the king is attacked and has no way out. Game over.
  • Stalemate — no legal move and not in check — the game is a draw.

The Three Phases of a Game

  • Opening (the first 10-15 moves or so) — get your pieces out, fight for the center, get your king castled to safety. This is where habits matter most.
  • Middlegame — most of the pieces are still on the board. This is where plans, attacks, and tactics like forks and pins happen.
  • Endgame — few pieces left. Kings come out to fight, pawns race to promote, and small technical ideas (like opposition) decide the game.
  • Every game moves through all three — a good player thinks a little differently in each one.

Grandpa's Teaching Philosophy

  • Learning is better with a warm person next to you — not a computer yelling answers.
  • Grandpa's method: ask, don't tell. "What do you think we should do?" — let the student think first.
  • Then gently guide: "Good move — but this one might have been even better. What do you think?"
  • It's a real, free-flowing conversation — type or talk, and the coach talks back out loud.

Opening Principles

  • Control the center, develop knights before bishops, castle early, connect your rooks.
  • Don't move the same piece twice in the opening, don't bring your queen out too early, don't hang pieces.
  • Don't memorize long lines — understand the idea behind each move.
  • Grandpa's favorite: 1.e4 e5 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 — a simple way to open the center fast.
  • Bobby Fischer — the 11th World Champion, crowned in 1972 — was famous for almost always opening with 1.e4, calling it "best by test."
  • Every opening move should have a reason: e4 fights for the center and opens the bishop and queen; Nf3 develops a piece and pressures e5.

Middlegame Plans

  • Open file for a rook — a file with no pawns on it lets a rook see the whole board.
  • Outpost for a knight — a square the opponent's pawns can never attack. A knight there is very strong.
  • The bishop pair — keeping both bishops is extra strong once the position opens up.
  • Space advantage — advanced pawns control more squares. Don't give that space back for free.
  • Pawn breaks — a pawn move that cracks open a closed position. Know when the moment is right.

Endgame Knowledge

  • Once most pieces are traded, the king becomes a fighting piece — bring him to the center.
  • Opposition — kings two squares apart, facing off. Whoever has to move first is at a disadvantage.
  • Passed pawn — no enemy pawns can stop it from queening. Push it quickly.
  • Rook behind the passed pawn — always stronger than a rook in front of it.
  • Lucena position — a winning technique (rook and pawn vs. rook) using a "bridge" to shield the king from checks.
  • Philidor position — the matching defensive technique, keeping the rook on the third rank to cut the king off.

Tactics Awareness

  • Fork — one piece attacks two at once. The knight fork is the most common.
  • Pin — a piece can't move because something valuable (often the king) is right behind it.
  • Skewer — like a pin in reverse: the valuable piece is in front and has to move, losing what's behind it.
  • Discovered attack — moving one piece out of the way reveals an attack from another.
  • Hanging piece — undefended and free to take. Always look for these first.
  • Back rank mate — the king is trapped on the last row by its own pawns.
  • Smothered mate — a knight delivers mate while the king is boxed in by its own pieces.
  • See the Tactics section for board diagrams — and now you can tap "Show me on the big board" to watch each one animated.

Time Management

  • Don't rush — take your time and really look at the board.
  • Good habits become automatic with practice: control the center, develop knights before bishops, castle early, take free pieces, and never leave a piece hanging.
  • The more you play, the faster you'll spot forks, pins, and hanging pieces — that's called pattern recognition.

Chess Ratings — What Is Elo?

  • A chess rating is just a number that estimates how strong a player is — the higher the number, the stronger the player.
  • It's called an Elo rating, named after Arpad Elo, the physics professor who invented the system in the 1960s.
  • Every player starts around 400-800 (a typical beginner on Chess.com or Lichess). Serious club players are usually 1200-1800. A Master is roughly 2200+. A Grandmaster (GM) is usually 2500+. The World Champion is usually around 2800.
  • The math: beat a player rated higher than you, and you gain more points than if you beat someone weaker. Lose to someone weaker, and you lose more points than losing to someone stronger.
  • Titles like IM (International Master) and GM (Grandmaster) are earned once, for life, by hitting rating and performance milestones — they never expire, even if the rating later drops.
  • Chess.com and Lichess both track a rating automatically as you play — it's a good, honest way to watch yourself improve over time.

📚 Where To Learn More

Books:

  • Bobby Fischer Teaches Chess — Bobby Fischer, Stuart Margulies & Donn Mosenfelder — a great first book, all puzzles.
  • Logical Chess: Move by Move — Irving Chernev — 33 full games explained one move at a time, in plain language.
  • My System — Aron Nimzowitsch — the classic on chess strategy, for once the basics feel comfortable.
  • Chess Fundamentals — José Raúl Capablanca — short, clear, written by a World Champion.
  • Silman's Complete Endgame Course — Jeremy Silman — endgame lessons organized by rating level, so you only study what you're ready for.

YouTube channels:

  • Chessbrah — GM Aman Hambleton's "Building Habits" series is one of the best step-by-step series for beginners.
  • John Bartholomew (IM) — his "Chess Fundamentals" series is excellent for beginners, clear and no wasted words.
  • GothamChess (IM Levy Rozman) — fun, clear explanations, great for all levels.
  • Saint Louis Chess Club — free lectures from real grandmasters.
  • Hanging Pawns — calm, well-organized lessons on openings and strategy.
  • Agadmator's Chess Channel — daily short, friendly walk-throughs of famous and current master games, move by move.
  • PowerPlayChess (GM Daniel King) — deeper, very clear breakdowns of grandmaster games.
  • ChessNetwork — instructive game analysis and puzzle solving.
  • Eric Rosen (IM) — relaxed, friendly games and lessons, good for beginners and intermediate players alike.
  • Watching real "master games" (games played by the world's best) is one of the best ways to learn — Agadmator and PowerPlayChess are mostly built around exactly that, explaining each move in plain language as they go.

Play online & take lessons:

  • Chess.com — play people your own level, puzzles, and structured lessons.
  • Lichess.org — 100% free, no ads — play, puzzles, and lessons too.
